corrected_value.title: Retrieval induces adaptive forgetting of competing memories via cortical pattern suppression

decisions.quote:
We therefore used
two criteria to assess whether we successfully replicated
Wimber et al.’s finding of forgetting for competitor images.
First, we used a posterior predictive check, generating the
range of plausible values for the average proportion correct in
each condition using the posteriors from the reanalysis of the
original data. If our replication data falls within the resulting
credible intervals, this indicates that the original estimates
can successfully predict new data from the same experi-
mental design.
decisions.location: Section 3.4 (Analyses for pre-registered design), page 35, lines 582-591 (and Reference list, page 45, lines 1182-1185)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind coding (target 0) identify Wimber, Alink, Charest, Kriegeskorte, & Anderson (2015), 'Retrieval induces adaptive forgetting of competing memories via cortical pattern suppression' (Nature Neuroscience, 18, 582-589, doi:10.1038/nn.3973), as the original study whose behavioral retrieval-induced forgetting paradigm and findings are directly re-tested.

decisions.quote:
Because this might
                                          reflect inadequate statistical power, we undertook two replication attempts of the
                                          behavioral paradigm, failing both times to observe more forgetting for competitors than
                                          targets. In fact, we failed to find any forgetting at all. We conclude that the study of Wimber
                                          et al. does not support the conclusion that forgetting is caused by targeted inhibition.
decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall failure verdict for their replication attempts of Wimber et al. (2015) in the title, abstract, results, and discussion: across all replication attempts (including the high-powered pre-registered direct replication and subgroup analyses), they failed to observe greater forgetting for competitors than targets or any forgetting effect at all on the final forced-choice recognition test. Qualitative replication of learning trends during the selective-retrieval phase does not alter the explicit overall failure verdict under Codebook Step 3, Rule 1.

decisions.reason: Although the paper also reanalyzes Wimber et al.'s (2015) original behavioral dataset (Section 4.1), it collects new behavioral data from independent participant samples across multiple replication experiments (Sections 2.1.2-2.1.3 and 4.2-4.4) to re-test Wimber et al.'s published behavioral retrieval-induced forgetting finding. Under Codebook Step 1, collecting new data in a different sample to re-test a previously published finding establishes the record type as 'replication'.
